extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetics/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic plots and characters: how to construct incidents, reversals, recognitions, catastrophes, and character psychology to provoke pity and fear in tragedy. Targets playwrights/novelists aiming to produce effective tragic fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination and aesthetic complement
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more attractions combined give greater pleasure than the separate values (the aesthetic value of a combined work can exceed the sum of its parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine salient features from originals or different sources to produce a greater unified aesthetic effect (example: an alabaster statue's value exceeds that of the alabaster and the sculpture separately). Use combination to heighten pleasure rather than merely juxtaposing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristicness to facilitate recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: An object/character is 'characteristic' when the characteristic marks of its species/variety are distinctly expressed; such characteristicness offers favourable conditions for recognition and so produces pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters and objects recognisable by clearly expressing their defining traits. Recognition should be neither trivial nor commonplace; it should be easy and precise enough to produce pleasurable judgment without lapsing into banality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of names and historical fidelity in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In Tragedy dramatists adhere to historical names because the potential (possibility) is a matter of faith; familiar historical names make improbable events seem possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, use known/historical names in tragic dramas to leverage audience belief in the possibility of events; avoid inventing crucial historical details that would undermine that faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance and definiteness of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The most agreeable stories are about what is neither extremely ancient nor quite modern; the definite is better known than the indefinite; a story about a single thing is more agreeable than one about many things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subject matter with a moderate temporal distance from the audience and focus plots on a single, definite sequence of events rather than sprawling multi-subject tales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as novelist — emphasis on imagination over versification
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should be the novelist rather than the versifier: imagination constitutes the poet, and the poet portrays imaginary chapters of life even when depicting past events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise imaginative construction of incidents and character over merely ornate verse or rhetorical display; treat dramatization as novelistic depiction of human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disjointed/simple (episodic) stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Of simple stories the disjointed are the worst; composing declamations and overstraining capacity often produces disjointed plots that are inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic, declamatory structures that force apart contiguous events. Aim for continuity and unity of action rather than a series of loosely connected episodes or declamatory set-pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid declamatory/overstrained rhetorical style for the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Declamation (repetition of the same thought in changed expression) is suitable for oratory and actors seeking 'speeches' but unsuitable for artistic writing where it causes disjointedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not design plots primarily to supply long declamatory speeches; the plot should serve the action, not episodic rhetorical display. Reserve tirades for cases where they are organically justified by character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for reversal (irony of fate) and recognition combined
rubrics_metrics.description: The best kind of plot is one in which recognition (disclosure of mistaken identity) is accompanied by the Irony of Fate (peripeteia); such combinations are most piteous or terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plots so that reversals and recognitions arise from the antecedents and yield strong emotional impact (e.g., Oedipus). Aim for recognition+reversal rather than isolated surprises or purely contrived twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidences should seem providential rather than blind chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences that look like providential 'chance'—chance which seems no blind chance—are preferable because they increase wonder while appearing plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using coincidences, craft them so they appear to follow moral certainty or law of nature, not sheer randomness (examples: murderer killed by falling statue). Avoid obvious contrivance that breaks audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must follow from antecedents by law or moral certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple or complex transitions should be deduced from the original structure of the story so that their occurrence comes about from antecedents by law of nature or moral certainty; there is a vast difference between sequel and consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that reversals, disclosures, and outcomes are motivated and necessary (or morally certain) given prior circumstances. Avoid sequences that are mere loose sequel without causal or moral grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Disclosure / Mistaken Identity as a central device
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of Mistaken Identity transforms a stranger into an acquaintance and is most effective when it affects the main characters; best when combined with Irony of Fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ identity-disclosure so it pivots the plot (e.g., revelation that changes relationships). Make such disclosures arise plausibly from antecedents and use them to produce pity or terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophe as necessary tragic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A Catastrophe is an experience involving destruction or pain (physical death, broken heart, mutilation, moral ruin); catastrophe is a component of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an appropriate form of catastrophe (physical or moral). Consider moral death or disgrace as valid tragic outcomes; choose the catastrophe that best fits the plot's moral and emotional trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical divisions of tragedy (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has separable members: Prologue, Scene, Finale, Chorus (with Introit and Stationary parts); Prologue = all before Chorus Introit; Scene = between choric odes; Finale = followed by no choric ode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure tragic works using these sections: establish context in the Prologue, proceed through Scenes delimited by choric odes, and conclude with a Finale. Use choric odes (Introit/Stationary) where appropriate to the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's proper subject — the terrible and the piteous
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the ideal tragedy should be complex and portray the terrible and the piteous; this is the peculiarity of tragedy and nothing else need do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the work on producing the specific aesthetic pleasure that arises from imagining woes and terrors—pity and fear—rather than on elements proper to comedy or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral status and cause of the hero's fall
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be neither a perfect paragon of virtue nor thoroughly wicked; the fall should be from good to ill and occasioned by a serious error (not by wickedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist of high status whose downfall stems from a mistake or error (hamartia) that elicits pity and fear. Avoid heroes who are wholly virtuous (uninspiring tragedy) or wholly villainous (elicits no pity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single rather than double plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed story must be single rather than double (not split into separate fates for virtuous and wicked characters); transition should be from good to ill, not from ill to good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate the dramatic energy on a single, unified plot line focused on the hero's reversal; avoid bifurcated narratives that dilute tragic impact by rewarding/punishing different groups separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity/fear through story, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Alarm and tears may be evoked by spectacle but more naturally and artistically by the story; dramatists should produce tragic gratification through portrayal of imaginary woes rather than expensive properties or monstrous spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely primarily on plotting, recognition, and character to produce pity and fear. Avoid cheap sensationalism or grotesque spectacle that does not belong to tragedy's proper effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity arises from relations — choose relational catastrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: Piteous experiences must be shared by connexions (relations), enemies, or neutrals; but catastrophes between members of the same family (brother/son/father/mother) are most piteous; killing an enemy or neutral produces little pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame tragic crimes and catastrophes among kin or close relations to maximise pity. Prefer familial or intimate relational contexts over impersonal victim-perpetrator relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect tradition but invent skilfully
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not violate traditional narratives (e.g., the murder of Clytaemnestra by Orestes) in vital parts; the poet should invent, but make skilful use of tradition to avoid deceiving the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use traditional or familiar stories as scaffolding but avoid altering essential, well-known elements that would provoke audience resentment. Small liberties in detail are permitted when they do not violate the salient features of the tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic handling of criminal intent (taxonomy of knowledge/action)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four basic cases regarding crime and knowledge: (1) know and not do (worst), (2) know and do (bad), (3) not know and do (better), (4) not know and not do (best). For drama, worst is conscious projection without perpetration; better is unconscious projection with perpetration followed by disclosure; best cases are those where discovery prevents the atrocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plots where crimes stem from ignorance or are averted by timely discovery (these elicit more pity and thrill). Avoid presenting conscious plotting without catastrophe (shocking but not moving) and prefer scenarios where disclosure or recognition transforms the moral outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation — four aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Four things should be aimed at in delineating character: (1) the characters should be good; (2) they should be appropriate (suitable to their sex/status/species); (3) they should be like (consistent with expected/known traits); (4) they should have equability (even if fitful, be uniformly fitful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters possess enough virtue to elicit sympathy, that their virtues/defects suit their social/natural kind, that portrayals respect audience expectations or historical likeness, and that temperament remains consistent throughout (no arbitrary 'unlike' moments). Examples of violations: unnecessary knavery, unseemly speeches, or sudden inconsistent behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and conduct must reveal intention and align with character
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or Conduct will be psychological if they reveal the intention behind actions; a character's goodness is judged by the intention expressed through speech/conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and action to make intentions intelligible and consistent with moral/natural laws. Avoid passages where speech or action contradict established character without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground character and incident in laws of nature and moral certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: In character and grouping of incidents, study laws of nature and moral certainty so that actions and transitions become necessary or morally certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor motivations and outcomes in psychologically and morally credible causes. Reversals and recognitions should feel necessary given human nature and previous events, not arbitrary contrivances.
